Summarizes prior evidence, the study's added value, and implications. It describes OASIS 1 as the first trial of an oral GLP-1 analogue for obesity and highlights the superior week-68 bodyweight reduction with oral semaglutide 50 mg versus placebo.

Describes the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 design, adult obesity eligibility criteria, 1:1 allocation, oral semaglutide dose escalation to 50 mg, common lifestyle intervention, coprimary endpoints, and treatment-policy estimand. Percentage bodyweight change at week 68 was analyzed by ANCOVA with multiple imputation in the full analysis set.

Reports results for 667 randomized participants. For the primary treatment-policy estimand at week 68, estimated mean percentage bodyweight change was −15.1% with oral semaglutide 50 mg and −2.4% with placebo, an estimated treatment difference of −12.7 percentage points (95% CI −14.2 to −11.3; p<0.0001).

Interprets oral semaglutide 50 mg as producing clinically meaningful weight loss superior to placebo, discusses consistency with subcutaneous semaglutide evidence, cardiometabolic effects and safety, and notes population generalizability and other trial limitations. content_sections.key_content_summary: Structured summary of the STEP 2 randomized phase 3 trial. It reports that semaglutide 2.4 mg reduced mean bodyweight by 9.6% versus 3.4% with placebo at week 68 (ETD −6.2 percentage points, 95% CI −7.3 to −5.2; p<0.0001), alongside categorical weight-loss and safety findings.

Explains the clinical importance of weight loss in adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes, reviews GLP-1 receptor agonists, and states the aim of evaluating weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg against semaglutide 1.0 mg and placebo for bodyweight management.

Summarizes prior evidence on anti-obesity GLP-1 therapies and describes the added value and implications of STEP 2. It highlights the observed week-68 weight reductions of 9.6%, 7.0%, and 3.4% with semaglutide 2.4 mg, semaglutide 1.0 mg, and placebo, respectively.

Describes the multicentre randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled design, eligibility criteria, 1:1:1 allocation, 68-week interventions plus lifestyle counseling, outcomes, and statistical analysis. The coprimary outcomes were percentage bodyweight change and achievement of at least 5% weight loss at week 68; the preferred treatment-policy estimand used intention-to-treat ANCOVA with multiple imputation for the continuous endpoint.

Reports results for 1210 randomized participants. For the synthesis-relevant outcome, mean percentage bodyweight change at week 68 was −9.6% with semaglutide 2.4 mg and −3.4% with placebo, yielding an adjusted treatment difference of −6.2 percentage points (95% CI −7.3 to −5.2; p<0.0001); additional categorical, metabolic, quality-of-life, and safety outcomes are also presented.

Interprets semaglutide 2.4 mg as significantly more effective than placebo and semaglutide 1.0 mg for reducing bodyweight in adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes. It contextualizes the 9.6% reduction and the 6.2-percentage-point advantage over placebo against other obesity pharmacotherapies and discusses cardiometabolic, quality-of-life, and safety findings.

content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarises the phase 3a randomised trial, eligibility, interventions, and outcomes. At week 68, semaglutide 2.4 mg and 1.7 mg produced greater percentage bodyweight reductions than placebo; it also reports visceral-fat and safety findings.

Explains obesity definitions and risks in east Asian populations, the importance of visceral adiposity, and the need for effective pharmacotherapy. Introduces the STEP programme and states the aim of evaluating weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo, with a 1.7 mg exploratory dose arm.
Reviews the lack of prior east Asian randomised trials of GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight management, describes the added value of STEP 6, and situates the findings within the wider evidence base.

Describes the multicentre double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled trial, randomisation, dosing, lifestyle co-intervention, outcomes, and statistical methods. Percentage bodyweight change and achievement of at least 5% weight loss at week 68 were coprimary outcomes; the primary treatment-policy estimand used ANCOVA with multiple imputation.

States that Novo Nordisk designed and oversaw the trial, monitored sites, analysed data, and funded medical writing and editorial support, while investigators handled clinical decisions and data collection.

Reports participant flow, baseline characteristics, efficacy, and safety. For the primary treatment-policy estimand at week 68, percentage bodyweight change was −13.2% with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus −2.1% with placebo (ETD −11.1 percentage points, 95% CI −12.9 to −9.2; p<0.0001); the 1.7 mg dose also outperformed placebo.

Interprets semaglutide-induced weight loss in east Asian adults with obesity and compares the magnitude with other STEP trials and weight-management pharmacotherapies. It emphasises the clinically meaningful bodyweight reductions and consistency with prior semaglutide evidence.

content_sections.key_content_summary: Structured abstract describing the 68-week randomized placebo-controlled STEP 9 trial. Semaglutide reduced percentage body weight more than placebo (−13.7% vs −3.2%; P<0.001) and also improved WOMAC pain and SF-36 physical function.

Reviews obesity-related knee osteoarthritis, the symptomatic benefits of weight reduction, and the need for effective pharmacologic weight management. Introduces STEP 9 as an assessment of whether semaglutide 2.4 mg is superior to placebo for reducing body weight and knee osteoarthritis pain.

Describes the multicenter double-blind randomized trial, eligibility criteria, 2:1 assignment to weekly subcutaneous semaglutide or placebo, lifestyle counseling, outcomes, and statistical analysis. Percentage change in body weight and change in WOMAC pain at week 68 were coprimary outcomes; the treatment-policy estimand in all randomized participants was used for confirmatory inference.

Reports participant flow and baseline characteristics, primary and secondary efficacy outcomes, and safety. For the synthesis outcome, mean percentage body-weight change at week 68 was −13.7% with semaglutide and −3.2% with placebo, with an estimated difference of −10.5 percentage points (95% CI, −12.3 to −8.6; P<0.001).

Interprets semaglutide as superior to placebo for reducing body weight and knee osteoarthritis pain and improving physical function. Discusses likely mechanisms, generalizability, limitations, and consistency of weight reduction and safety with prior STEP trials.

content_sections.section_title: Abstract (IMPORTANCE / OBJECTIVE / DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS / INTERVENTIONS / MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES / RESULTS / CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE)
content_sections.key_content_summary: Reports a 68-week randomized trial of semaglutide 2.4 mg, liraglutide 3.0 mg, and matched placebo in 338 adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes. Mean percentage body-weight change was −15.8% with semaglutide, −6.4% with liraglutide, and −1.9% with pooled placebo; semaglutide was superior to liraglutide on the primary and confirmatory weight-loss outcomes.

Introduces semaglutide and liraglutide as GLP-1 receptor agonists used for chronic weight management and explains their pharmacologic differences. Motivates STEP 8 as a direct efficacy and safety comparison of weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg with daily liraglutide 3.0 mg.
Umbrella section describing the STEP 8 phase 3b randomized trial design, participants, interventions, outcomes, sample-size planning, and statistical analysis.
Describes a 68-week randomized, open-label trial conducted at 19 US sites, with ethical oversight and written informed consent.

Defines eligibility as adults with BMI at least 30, or at least 27 with a weight-related comorbidity, and prior unsuccessful dietary weight-loss efforts. Key exclusions included diabetes, HbA1c at least 6.5%, and recent substantial weight change.
Summarizes the clinical question and central finding: mean body-weight change at 68 weeks was −15.8% with semaglutide versus −6.4% with liraglutide, indicating greater weight loss with semaglutide.

Details 3:1:3:1 randomization to weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg or matching placebo and daily liraglutide 3.0 mg or matching placebo for 68 weeks. All groups also received counseling for a 500-kcal/day deficit and at least 150 minutes/week of physical activity.

Defines percentage change from baseline in body weight at week 68 as the primary endpoint. Semaglutide-versus-placebo and liraglutide-versus-placebo comparisons were prespecified supportive secondary comparisons; responder thresholds and other cardiometabolic outcomes were also specified.

Describes hierarchical superiority testing and assumptions used to power active-treatment comparisons, including more than 90% power for semaglutide versus liraglutide. The pooled placebo group was planned to provide more than 99% power for semaglutide versus placebo on the primary endpoint.

Specifies the treatment-policy estimand as primary, ANCOVA for continuous endpoints, logistic regression for binary endpoints, and multiple imputation for missing data. Analyses included all randomized participants; only primary and confirmatory semaglutide-versus-liraglutide endpoints were multiplicity controlled.

Umbrella results section reporting participant disposition, baseline characteristics, percentage and absolute body-weight outcomes, categorical weight-loss outcomes, supportive cardiometabolic outcomes, and treatment discontinuation.

Reports enrollment of 338 participants (126 semaglutide, 127 liraglutide, 85 pooled placebo), baseline characteristics, and follow-up. Overall, 94.4% completed the trial, 80.2% completed treatment, and 92.3% had a week-68 body-weight assessment.

At week 68, estimated mean percentage body-weight change was −15.8% with semaglutide and −6.4% with liraglutide; the adjusted difference was −9.4 percentage points (95% CI, −12.0 to −6.8; P<.001). The abstract additionally reports −1.9% for pooled placebo.
Semaglutide produced significantly higher odds than liraglutide of achieving at least 10%, 15%, and 20% weight loss at week 68; all comparisons had P<.001.

Reports discontinuation and supportive efficacy outcomes. Semaglutide reduced absolute weight, waist circumference, and several cardiometabolic measures more than liraglutide; the provided excerpt is truncated during these results.
